name: P. F. W. Peck's Store
aka: Peck's store at South Water and LaSalle

documented_range.note: THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A SOURCE PUTS THIS BUILDING IN EXISTENCE, NOT ITS BUILD DATE. Andreas has the Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging in the store's unfinished loft in May 1833, so the building stood and was already a store then; this project's own dossier dates the store '1832-33' (docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 5) and no source reached fixes a month or a year for its erection. Peck himself arrived in July 1831 with goods in the schooner Telegraph and was a licensed merchant, so a store of his could be a year older than this range says. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR AND IT IS STRONGER HERE THAN ON MOST RECORDS IN THIS DATASET: Andreas has Peck still advertising dry goods, hardware and groceries in 1834-35 and still LIVING at the store, and this project's own data/exclusions.json says so in the entry that keeps his 1837 brick house out of the scene. What is not attested is when the building came down; 1835-12-31 is a housekeeping bound, not a demolition date.

change_note: The two-storey frame store P. F. W. Peck kept at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle, and lived in: dry goods, hardware and groceries below, an unfinished loft above that served as lodging. It is the building this project models Peck at on 1835-07-01, because his two-storey dwelling at LaSalle and Washington belongs to an 1837 description and his brick house is 1837 — both already recorded in data/exclusions.json.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half — the same reading the Sauganash and the Green Tree carry. Andreas puts Peck's store at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle. METHOD, the project's standard one: South Water Street is today's East and West Wacker Drive along the south bank of the main stem, the equivalence this project's own dossier states in its street-name key (docs/research/03-structures-north.md), and LaSalle Street is unchanged. The modern West Upper Wacker Drive / North LaSalle Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 447525.2, N 4637408.1 (three nodes averaged, spread 15.4 m, fetched 2026-08-11), and the footprint origin set 12.2 m west and 12.2 m south of it less the building's own width and depth, so that the store's north face sits on the South Water frontage and its east face on the LaSalle frontage of a south-west corner lot. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M, which is the georeference's residual (data/datum.json: 17.5 m RMS on Wright 1834, with 3.7 per cent paper stretch), not an additional guess. TWO SOURCES OF ERROR ON TOP OF THAT, BOTH RECORDED RATHER THAN AVERAGED AWAY. First, the 12.2 m offset is half of an 80 ft street, the width annotated on Hathaway 1834, while Currey states the 1830 Thompson plat laid streets out 'uniformly 66 feet wide'; the difference is 2.1 m per offset and is already recorded in docs/RESEARCH/hogan_store.md § 5. Second, and larger, MODERN WACKER DRIVE IS NOT EXACTLY THE 1835 SOUTH WATER STREET LINE: Wacker was built on South Water's right of way in 1924-26 and widened northward over the old dock line. As a check, this project's own traced 1834 south bank (data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson) runs 41.6 m north of this record's north face at this easting, which is about the right room for a street and a river frontage and puts the building on ground the trace shows as land. Facade bearing 0, due north onto South Water, INFERRED FROM THE STREET RATHER THAN FROM ANY STATEMENT: nothing says which way the store faced, and a corner store fronting LaSalle instead would rotate it 90 degrees.
placement.symbolic_location: South-west corner of South Water Street and LaSalle Street (today the south side of West Wacker Drive at North LaSalle Street), on the commercial core block between LaSalle and Clark.

footprint.note: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION. What IS documented is a cap on one of them: Andreas states that South Water Street lots were 55 ft wide (docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 5), so a store on a single lot on this street cannot have had more than 55 ft of frontage, and this rectangle's 40 ft frontage sits comfortably inside that. The two numbers are borrowed rather than freshly invented, and that is deliberate: 40 ft is the frontage attested for the Green Tree Tavern and for the Western Hotel's front, and 25 ft is the depth derived from the Green Tree's attested room module — the only period figures for a commercial building this dataset actually holds. So the shape is a claim about the TYPE and not about this building. 12.192 x 7.62 m is 40 x 25 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per data/datum.json's units rule. The same rectangle is used on four records in this parcel; that repetition is the honest form of the admission, not an accident.

stories.note: Andreas: a two-story frame store. The unfinished loft over those two storeys is stated separately as `loft` and is not counted here — the storey count is the finished, floored accommodation, which is what the archetype extrudes wall height from.

loft.note: THE SINGLE MOST VIVID DOCUMENTED FACT ABOUT THIS BUILDING. Andreas has an 'unfinished loft' over the two storeys, used as lodging: the Rev. Jeremiah Porter, arriving in May 1833 to found what became the First Presbyterian church, slept in it. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED IS THAT THE LOFT WAS THERE AND THAT IT WAS UNFINISHED IN MAY 1833. Whether it was still unfinished twenty-six months later on the scene date is NOT attested, and this record does not claim it — `framing_exposed` is deliberately not stated, because the archetype would then leave the loading gable open and show a visitor a building site two years after the one moment anybody described. The archetype builds a loft as one gable opening and nothing else, which is the honest external trace of a loft.

construction.note: Andreas says 'frame' and no more, and the word does not distinguish the two methods available. Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and became the dominant local method within a few years; this building's date is not fixed and may precede that, so braced frame is the safer reading, exactly as the Sauganash record argues for 1831. The alternative is real and this note is where it is recorded rather than in a footnote: if the store went up in 1833 it could as easily have been balloon framed, and nothing reached decides it.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 5.5 m is about 18 ft: two 8 ft storeys plus floor structure and a low sill course, the same reading and the same number this project gives the Sauganash, which is the other two-storey frame building it models. What is inferred is that the height falls in this range, not that it is exactly 5.5 m. It excludes the unfinished loft, which would add a knee wall of unknown height under the roof.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for frame buildings of this type, period and region, and a building with a habitable loft under the roof is gabled by type. Typological derivation, not a measurement.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for this building. 33 degrees is the frame_storefront archetype's own figure for a store, and it is adopted here rather than the 38 this project uses for taverns because the archetype argues the case from the dataset's one attested store footprint: a store's frontage is long and its plan shallow, so a tavern's pitch puts more roof above the eave than there is wall below it and the building stops reading as a shop. Inferred from construction practice and from the type, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested, and nothing describes a stack on this building at all. One is the minimum for a store kept through Chicago winters with its owner living in it. The COUNT is the inference; where the stack stands, how big it is and what it is made of are the archetype's, which is the standing admission in docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

function.note: Both halves are attested and they are attested separately. The store: Peck was a licensed merchant advertising dry goods, hardware and groceries through 1834-35. The dwelling: Andreas has Peck living at the store, and this project's exclusion of his 1837 brick house rests on exactly that reading. The loft over the two storeys was let for lodging at least once, to the Rev. Jeremiah Porter in May 1833.

occupants.value: Philip F. W. Peck, merchant, and his household
occupants.note: Peck arrived at Chicago in July 1831 with a stock of goods in the schooner Telegraph and was among the town's first licensed merchants. He is attested keeping this store and living in it across 1833-35. No source reached names a clerk, a partner or a lodger at the scene date; the Porter lodging is May 1833 and is not carried forward as an 1835 occupancy.

residents.name: The Peck household
residents.why: A merchant of this period lived over or behind his store, and this one demonstrably housed a lodger in its loft. Not stated of Peck himself.

persons.name: Philip F. W. Peck
persons.note: HIS UNFINISHED LOFT IS THE PARCEL'S BEST DOCUMENTED LODGING. Andreas: 'Among these was P. F. W. Peck, who invited Mr. Porter to make his temporary lodging place and study in the unfinished loft of his two-story store'; and 'The first building in the rear of this store was the log house of Rufus Brown, where Mr. Porter found table board.' Three households and two buildings meet in those two sentences. He arrived in July 1831 with a stock of goods carried by schooner, per this project's building record. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named'.

residents.research_note: THE HOUSEHOLD AT THE CENTRE OF A THREE-WAY LINK. Peck's store lodged the Presbyterian minister in its loft and Rufus Brown's log boarding house stood directly behind it - so a single corner of South Water and LaSalle carries a merchant, a minister and a boarding-house keeper, all documented, all in this parcel. That is the density the inferred phase should expect to find everywhere and can only demonstrate here.

residents.name: The Porter household
residents.why: ONE OF ONLY TWO DOCUMENTED RESIDENCE LINKS IN THIS PARCEL, and it is a lodging rather than a home. Andreas: 'Among these was P. F. W. Peck, who invited Mr. Porter to make his temporary lodging place and study in the unfinished loft of his two-story store, standing on the southwest corner of South Water and LaSalle streets.' data/structures/peck_store.json independently records the unfinished loft used as lodging. THE WORD 'TEMPORARY' IS IN THE SOURCE and this link is dated 1833; whether he was still in the loft in 1835, and whether he took his wife there, is unknown.

persons.name: Rev. Jeremiah Porter
persons.note: THE HOUSEHOLD THAT TURNED UP THE PARCEL'S SHARPEST DATE PROBLEM. Andreas: 'In the spring of 1835, Mr. Porter was chosen by the Presbytery of Ottawa its first delegate to the General Assembly which met that spring in Pittsburgh. After the adjournment of the Assembly, Mr. Porter was married, at Rochester, N. Y., to Miss Eliza Chappel, then late of Chicago, and with his wife visited his parents who were living in Massachusetts.' The marriage is dated elsewhere in the same volume to 15 June 1835 - SIXTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, at Rochester, New York. Andreas also says he stayed 'until Mr. Porter left Chicago, in September, 1835'. So he is the town's Presbyterian minister on 1 July 1835 and may well have been eight hundred miles away that morning.

persons.name: Eliza Chappel Porter
persons.note: MARRIED SIXTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE AND DESCRIBED BY ANDREAS AS 'THEN LATE OF CHICAGO' AT THE TIME OF THE WEDDING - which is a statement that she had already left the town. Her school had moved out of the State Street log house in 1834. She is carried in this household under her married name because that is her status on 1 July 1835, and the household's presence field records what follows from it.

residents.research_note: THE RECORD THAT PROVES THE presence FIELD EARNS ITS KEEP. Jeremiah Porter is, on any reading, a documented Chicago resident of 1835 and the town's Presbyterian minister; and the best evidence this project holds puts him at a wedding in western New York sixteen days before the scene date and on a family visit in Massachusetts after it. Without a presence field the dataset would have had to either drop him or assert him, and both would be wrong. A SECOND CONSEQUENCE, ALREADY IN THE STRUCTURES LAYER: the church record's refusal to name a minister as its occupant now has a reason attached to it, which is the kind of loop the residents programme is meant to close.

citations.citation: Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time. Vol. 1. Chicago: A. T. Andreas, 1884.
OpenStreetMap contributors. Street centerline intersection nodes for downtown Chicago, retrieved via the Overpass API, 2026-08-09.

research_note: THE ANCHOR OF THE SOUTH WATER STREET COMMERCIAL ROW, and the first store this dataset has ever held on the street that was the town's business street. Andreas gives three things plainly — a two-storey frame store, the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle, and an unfinished loft over it used as lodging — and gives no dimension at all, which is why the footprint is invented inside the one documented constraint the street offers: 55 ft lots. THE LOFT IS THE PART OF THIS RECORD THAT IS DOCUMENTED AND NOT BUILT, and it is worth stating in full because a visitor cannot see it. Rev. Jeremiah Porter, arriving in May 1833 to found what became the First Presbyterian Church, lodged in the unfinished loft of this store; that is the kind of detail that makes a boom-town store legible, and the model shows a plain two-storey block with a roof over it and nothing of the loft. It is not stated as a form attribute because the frame_storefront archetype was being written in parallel with this record and no record should guess at a parameter vocabulary that does not exist yet — the moment that archetype lands with a loft parameter, this record should gain 'loft': {value: true, confidence: 'documented'} and lose this paragraph. See docs/RESEARCH/peck_store.md. DO NOT ADD PECK'S BRICK HOUSE TO THIS SCENE: it is 1837, it is the first brick house erected in Chicago, and it is already in data/exclusions.json.
